\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{कृष्णः} (kṛṣṇaḥ)}{कृष्णः (kṛṣṇaḥ)}]{\sk{कृष्णः} (kṛṣṇaḥ) — black, dark}

\label{lesson:SA-C131-krsnah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for weak, then the Sanskrit for clear.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कृष्णः}}
\textbf{\sk{कृष्णः}} — \emph{kṛṣṇaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}black, dark\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{kṛṣṇa} \textquotedblleft{}black, dark\textquotedblright{} is old, in the Rigveda, and is inherited from Indo-European; Old Prussian \emph{kirsnan} \textquotedblleft{}black\textquotedblright{} is a cousin (EtymDB). As a name it is Krishna, \textquotedblleft{}the dark one\textquotedblright{}, whom Hindi calls \emph{kānh} (CDIAL 3451).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kṛṣṇaḥ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kṛṣṇaḥ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{kṛṣṇaḥ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for weak, then the Sanskrit for clear, then say \emph{kṛṣṇaḥ} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{धूसरः} (dhūsaraḥ)}{धूसरः (dhūsaraḥ)}]{\sk{धूसरः} (dhūsaraḥ) — grey}

\label{lesson:SA-C131-dhusarah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for clear, then the Sanskrit for black.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{धूसरः}}
\textbf{\sk{धूसरः}} — \emph{dhūsaraḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}grey\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dhūsara} \textquotedblleft{}dust-coloured, grey\textquotedblright{} is linked by CDIAL 6870 with words for dust, while MW suggests the root √dhvaṃs \textquotedblleft{}fall to dust\textquotedblright{}; its exact formation is uncertain. Hindi and Marathi kept it as \emph{dhūsar} \textquotedblleft{}grey\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 6870).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{पाटलः} (pāṭalaḥ)}{पाटलः (pāṭalaḥ)}]{\sk{पाटलः} (pāṭalaḥ) — pink}

\label{lesson:SA-C131-patalah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for black, then the Sanskrit for grey.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{पाटलः}}
\textbf{\sk{पाटलः}} — \emph{pāṭalaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}pink\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{pāṭala} \textquotedblleft{}pale red, pink\textquotedblright{} also names the trumpet-flower tree (MW). Neither MW nor CDIAL 8033 gives a derivation, so its origin is uncertain; DEDR 4075 compares Dravidian names for that tree.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{स्पष्टः} (spaṣṭaḥ)}{स्पष्टः (spaṣṭaḥ)}]{\sk{स्पष्टः} (spaṣṭaḥ) — clear}

\label{lesson:SA-C131-spastah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for grey, then the Sanskrit for pink.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{स्पष्टः}}
\textbf{\sk{स्पष्टः}} — \emph{spaṣṭaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}clear\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{spaṣṭa} \textquotedblleft{}clearly perceived, distinct\textquotedblright{} belongs to the root √spaś \textquotedblleft{}see, spy\textquotedblright{} (MW), inherited from Indo-European (EtymDB). MW sets √spaś beside Greek \emph{skeptomai}, Latin \emph{specio} and English \emph{spy}.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{स्थूलः} (sthūlaḥ)}{स्थूलः (sthūlaḥ)}]{\sk{स्थूलः} (sthūlaḥ) — thick, fat}

\label{lesson:SA-C131-sthulah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for pink, then the Sanskrit for clear.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{स्थूलः}}
\textbf{\sk{स्थूलः}} — \emph{sthūlaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}thick, fat\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sthūla} \textquotedblleft{}large, thick, stout\textquotedblright{} comes, according to MW, from √sthū, a form of √sthā \textquotedblleft{}stand\textquotedblright{}: \textquotedblleft{}solid, firm-standing\textquotedblright{}. It is old, in the Atharvaveda, and lives on as Punjabi \emph{ṭhullhā} \textquotedblleft{}fat, coarse\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 13776).
\end{cousinweb}
